title: Unit final: data structure design
sub: New problems to recognize, an LRU trace with predictions, a trap, formats, a replay buffer and explaining out loud
cards/0/q: New problems. Match each statement with how the structure is built.
cards/0/pairs/0/0: Add and Search Words (#211): '.' in a query is any letter
cards/0/pairs/0/1: A trie; on a dot, walk all children
cards/0/pairs/1/0: Moving Average (#346): the average of the last size numbers of a stream
cards/0/pairs/1/1: A ring of size slots and a running sum
cards/0/pairs/2/0: All O(1) Data Structure (#432): inc, dec, the key with the largest and smallest count
cards/0/pairs/2/1: Buckets by count, as in LFU
cards/0/pairs/3/1: A list + a dictionary of indices, delete by swapping with the last
cards/0/pairs/4/0: Save a graph where objects reference each other in a cycle
cards/0/pairs/4/1: Ids instead of references, loading in two passes
cards/1/q: Design Add and Search Words (#211): addWord(word) and search(word), where a dot in word is any letter. Length up to 25, at most two dots per query, up to 10⁴ addWord and search calls in total. How do you search?
cards/1/options/0: A trie: on a letter, one edge; on a dot, recursively every existing child of the node
cards/1/options/1: A HashSet<string>, and on a query with a dot, scan all words comparing character by character
cards/1/options/2: A trie, skipping the dot: search for the word without it
cards/1/options/3: Sort the words and binary search for the first one with that beginning
cards/1/explain: Without dots the search is an ordinary path through the trie, O(L). A dot branches the walk into every existing child, not into 26 hypothetical ones: branches with no edge drop out at once. With two dots that is at most 26² paths of 25 letters — and usually far fewer.
cards/1/wrong/1: Scanning all words is up to n · 25 character comparisons per query: with 5000 words and 5000 queries that is 6·10⁸.
cards/1/wrong/2: A dot is exactly one letter, not an empty spot: “b.d” matches “bad” but not “bd”.
cards/1/wrong/3: The dot can come first: “.ad”. A sorted array only helps with a known beginning.
cards/2/task: A new sequence for an LRU cache of 2 keys. The most recent is on the left. The rig will ask twice whom the code evicts.
cards/2/goal/asks/0/q: get(1) made key 1 the most recent, then put(2, 20) arrived. Whom does put(3, 3) evict?
cards/2/goal/asks/0/explain: put(2, 20) is an update and also a use: key 2 moved to the front, and 1 ended up at the tail. The tail is evicted — key 1, even though it was read recently. An update frees no room: there are still two keys.
cards/2/goal/asks/1/q: get(1) missed, get(2) returned 20. Whom does put(4, 4) evict?
cards/2/goal/asks/1/explain: A miss changes nothing, and get(2) moved 2 to the front: the list is 2, 3. The tail is key 3 — inserted after key 2, but not touched since. Recency counts from the last use, not from the insertion.
cards/3/q: Capacity 2: Put(1, 1), Put(2, 2), Get(1), Put(3, 3), Get(1). The last Get returned −1, but it should return 1. Tap the buggy line.
cards/3/explain: The front of the list is the most recent, the back is the victim. Get moves the node it read to the back, right into the line of fire: after Get(1) the list is 2, 1, and Put(3, 3) drops the key 1 that was just read. It needs AddFirst(node), as in Put.
cards/4/q: Unity: a replay of the last 10 seconds at 60 FPS. A frame's state is a 48-byte struct, written every frame. What do you use?
cards/4/options/0: A ring of 1024 slots with overwrite and a mask index: 48 KB, no allocations
cards/4/options/1: A List<FrameState>: Add at the end and RemoveAt(0) once there are more than 600 frames
cards/4/options/2: A LinkedList<FrameState>: AddLast and RemoveFirst are both O(1)
cards/4/options/3: A ring of 600 slots will not do: without a power of two some frames are lost
cards/4/explain: 600 frames round up to a power of two — 1024, and the index is tail & 1023. 1024 · 48 bytes = 48 KB, allocated once. 600 slots with % would work as well: the mask is an optimization, not a correctness requirement.
cards/4/wrong/1: RemoveAt(0) shifts all 600 structs every frame — 28 KB of copying for one frame. A ring shifts nothing.
cards/4/wrong/2: Every AddLast is a new heap node, 60 objects of garbage per second for Boehm. A ring on an array produces none.
cards/4/wrong/3: With %, a ring of 600 slots is perfectly correct. A power of two only turns a division into a bitwise AND.
cards/5/q: Serialize and Deserialize N-ary Tree (#428): a node has between 0 and N children. Which formats rebuild the tree unambiguously? Select all.
cards/5/options/0: Pre-order: the value, the number of children, then the children in order
cards/5/options/1: Pre-order: the value, the children, then a # marker for “no more children”
cards/5/options/3: Only the values by levels, with no markers
cards/5/explain: The principle is the same as for a binary tree: the shape must be written explicitly. A binary node has exactly two child slots, so # in an empty slot was enough. An N-ary node has a varying number of children: you either write that number up front or close the list of children with a marker. Values without shape information lose it under any traversal.
cards/6/q: Your own save format: units reference their squad, and the squad references the list of its units. How do you write and load it?
cards/6/options/0: Give every object an id and write references as numbers; loading: create all objects, then link them by id
cards/6/options/1: Pre-order with # markers, as for a tree
cards/6/options/2: Write the squad inside every unit — Unity will sort out the duplicates
cards/6/options/3: Save only the units and recreate the squads empty
cards/6/explain: This is a graph with a cycle: unit → squad → unit. Following references without visited marks never stops, and writing by value multiplies the squad into copies. Ids and two passes on load handle both shared references and cycles.
cards/6/wrong/1: Markers describe a tree. On the cycle unit → squad → unit the walk goes round forever.
cards/6/wrong/2: By value, every unit gets its own copy of the squad, and the cycle is cut off at depth 10.
cards/6/wrong/3: The squads' data and the links are lost — that is not a save, it is a restart.
cards/7/q: You are solving Add and Search Words out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/7/items/0: Clarify: which characters, how many dots per query, how many words and queries
cards/7/items/1: Name the naive solution: scan all words comparing character by character — O(n · L) per query
cards/7/items/2: The idea: a trie; on a letter, one edge; on a dot, walk all children of the node
cards/7/items/3: Write addWord as Insert, and search as a recursion over the position in the word
cards/7/items/4: Walk an example: bad, dad, mad and the queries .ad and b..
cards/7/items/5: Complexity: addWord is O(L); search is O(L) without dots, up to 26 branches at each dot
cards/7/items/6: Edge cases: a query of only dots, a query longer than any word
cards/7/explain: The number of dots is the key question: the worst case of the search depends on it. The rest follows the trie pattern, but search is recursive: it branches only on a dot.
cards/8/q: Complexity and cost of this unit's structures. What is true? Select all.
cards/8/options/0: LRU on a dictionary and a doubly linked list: Get and Put are O(1) on average
cards/8/options/1: LFU with buckets and minFreq is O(1) on average, and with a SortedSet by (freq, tick) it is O(log n)
cards/8/options/2: Search in a trie is O(L) and does not depend on the number of words
cards/8/options/3: Serialization with markers is 2n + 1 tokens and O(n) both ways
cards/8/options/4: DeQueue in a circular queue is O(k): the elements shift towards the start
cards/8/options/5: StartsWith on a HashSet<string> is O(L): the prefix is found by its hash
cards/8/explain: The first four sum up the unit. A ring shifts nothing: DeQueue moves head, O(1). And the hash of a prefix has nothing to do with the hashes of the words: StartsWith on a HashSet is a scan, O(n · L).
